directions.direction: Adopt the cluster's positive typed domain-patch projection, and source it from the shared Zod contract rather than hand-listing fields in the client. In packages/shared/src/schemas/{inventory-inputs.ts,character-inputs.ts}, split each affected mutation input into a positive entity-patch schema (e.g. inventoryItemPatchSchema, characterStatsPatchSchema, characterPersonalityPatchSchema containing only persisted-entity fields) and recompose the existing wire input as patchSchema.extend({ id/characterId, campaignId, expectedVersion }).strict(), exporting the inferred patch types — wire validation semantics must stay byte-identical. In the client, each writer's onMutate builds its cache patch via the patch schema's default strip-mode parse (Zod 4 plain objects strip unknown keys), e.g. const patch: InventoryItemPatch = inventoryItemPatchSchema.parse(variables); this is a positive, typed, assertion-free projection where control fields (id, characterId, campaignId injected by useCampaignScopedMutation, expectedVersion) can never reach cached rows, and any future control field added to the input via .extend is stripped automatically with no denylist to maintain. Replace use-inventory.ts's { ...i, ...variables } spread, delete UPDATE_STATS_CONTROL_FIELDS plus buildUpdateStatsPatch's Record<string, unknown> return (type applyStatsPatch against the new patch type; the version-increment logic stays where it is), and replace personality's id-filter with its patch parse; a tiny shared projection helper in cache-helpers.ts is optional if it stays a one-liner. Add regression tests beside each hook asserting cached rows contain no campaignId/expectedVersion/characterId after an optimistic update, plus a shared-schema parity test (the repo's existing .shape/toMatchObject idiom, cf. spell-action-inputs.test.ts) asserting each input schema's shape equals patch shape plus its declared control fields. Out of scope: any change to server routers/services, to wire validation behavior, to useCampaignScopedMutation itself, and to the other optimistic writers (spells, rest, spell-slots, sorcery-points, weapon-masteries) whose patches are already hand-built positive objects — the convention note may name them as the pattern to follow, but refactoring them is not part of this leaf.

Calling patchSchema.parse inside onMutate introduces a client-side runtime parse that throws on contract drift where the old spread silently passed data through; since variables were already schema-shaped this is low-probability, but a throw in onMutate aborts the optimistic update path and should be covered by a test. directions.direction: Keep the cluster's test spine — for each of the five endpoints, seed multiple pages containing several rows that share the boundary sort tuple, traverse pages until nextCursor is null, and assert the exact ordered ID sequence with no omissions or duplicates — but the leaf must also carry the production fixes those tests will force, and must distinguish the two production shapes. For chat (packages/server/src/routers/chat.ts:185-188), notification (routers/notification.ts:28), and combat-log (services/encounter-combat/combat-log.ts:92-99), the cursor is a bare timestamp with no tie-breaker, so the new tie tests will fail against current code: converge them on the id-cursor idiom the repo already uses in magic-item/monster — Prisma `cursor: { id: lastItem.id }, skip: 1` with orderBy extended to end in id ([createdAt desc, id desc] for chat/notification; [round asc, createdAt asc, id asc] for combat-log, keeping round-major order). The wire cursor stays an opaque z.string (nextCursor becomes an id instead of an ISO timestamp); client infinite queries round-trip nextCursor opaquely via getNextPageParam, so no shared-schema or client change is needed. For magic-item and monster the cursor value is already a unique id; the gap is a non-total orderBy — append `id: "asc"` as the terminal orderBy key and add duplicate-name (and duplicate-CR+name) fixtures straddling a page boundary. Tie fixtures must be seeded via direct Prisma inserts with explicitly pinned equal createdAt values (extend the notification-test-helper seeding pattern; chat's HTTP sendMessage path cannot force equal timestamps), and each tie test should assert the tie precondition by reading back the seeded timestamps so the case cannot go vacuously green. Follow TDD: land the failing tie tests first, then the cursor fixes, in one leaf. Out of scope: client cache/infinite-query changes, whisper-visibility filtering, offset-style pagination elsewhere, and any redesign of the shared cursor input schemas.
directions.risks: Changing chat/notification/combat-log nextCursor payloads from timestamps to ids invalidates any persisted or in-flight cursors and would break any consumer that parses the cursor as a date — grep client and server for cursor parsing before landing (current getNextPageParam usage is opaque, but re-verify at implementation time). Combat-log's round-major ordering is the trap: an id cursor without round retained ahead of createdAt in orderBy interleaves rounds, and equal-createdAt-across-different-round rows are the case most likely to be mis-fixed. Seeded "equal" timestamps can silently diverge (DB defaults or timestamp precision), letting tie tests pass without ever exercising a tie — hence the mandatory tie-precondition assertion.

directions.direction: Take the supervised-runner branch of the proposed direction and drop the disposable-worktree branch: in-place is load-bearing for all three lanes (sandbox/worktree copies break vitest global-setup resolution, git-dependent script tests, and @musi/lint-ratchet resolution per each config's comments), and per-run worktree provisioning (bun install + per-worktree DB/Redis via worktree:init) is L-shaped, not M. Replace the four inline bash wrappers in package.json (test:mutation, test:server:mutation, test:scripts:mutation, test:lint-ratchet:mutation) with one shared runner script (e.g. scripts/mutation-run.sh or a Bun TS entry under scripts/, TDD-able like the other scripts) that takes the lane config path, imports it to obtain the lane's mutate globs, and wraps `stryker run`. The runner does three things: (1) preflight — resolve the mutate globs to tracked files and abort if any have staged or unstaged modifications, mirroring the existing verify:changed abort-on-unstaged idiom; this is the guarantee that stranded mutants can never mix with legitimate uncommitted work; (2) stale-state detection — at startup, if `.stryker-tmp/backup` exists or the mutate-target paths are dirty (impossible given preflight of a prior supervised run, therefore evidence of an interrupted run), refuse to start and print the exact recovery command (`git restore --worktree -- <paths>` plus `.stryker-tmp` removal), or restore automatically behind an explicit flag; (3) keep the existing stryker-setup-*.js EXIT/INT/TERM trap and extend it to restore mutate-target paths on abnormal exit — while documenting in the runner that traps cannot fire on SIGKILL/OOM, so startup detection, not the trap, is the rail for the hard-kill case the configs describe. Update the three lane-config comments to point at the runner as the recovery rail instead of just acknowledging the risk. Explicitly out of scope: any change to stryker.shared.mjs's lane-option contract or inPlace semantics (CQ25-221/leaf 43 territory), sandbox/worktree migration, and the operator-doc rewrite owned by D-116.
directions.risks: The restore-on-exit path is itself a data-loss hazard if the restored path set ever diverges from what preflight verified clean — the runner must restore only a file list it recorded at preflight time, never a re-evaluated glob. Glob resolution must match Stryker's semantics (including the `!` exclusions) or preflight silently under-covers and detection under-fires; a small test pinning resolved sets for all three lanes guards this. Over-strict preflight (requiring the whole tree clean rather than just mutate targets) would regress DX for overnight runs on fast-commit branches with unrelated uncommitted work.
directions.sequencing: Land before D-116 (L07-112): its doc correction explicitly coordinates wording with this candidate and must describe the final runtime behavior (preflight, stale detection, recovery command). directions.direction: Keep the cluster direction, concretized in three moves. (1) Give login-route.ts a validateSearch producing `{ returnTo?: string }` by delegating to the existing `isSafeReturnTo` in packages/client/src/lib/login-redirect.ts, mirroring the repo's established pattern in packages/client/src/routes/campaign-detail-route.ts (register-route.ts, also wrapped by GuestGuard, gets the same validateSearch so the guard's read path is uniform). (2) AuthGuard then drops the dual-prop `<Navigate to="/login" href={buildLoginHref(...)} />` in favor of typed navigation: `<Navigate to="/login" search={returnTo ? { returnTo } : {}} />`, with the safe-target check happening once in the search contract rather than via a hand-built href. (3) GuestGuard's resume — the one destination that genuinely cannot be a typed route literal — moves into a single small adapter (e.g. `ResumeNavigate` beside the guards or in lib/), which reads the validated `returnTo` from route search and renders href-only `<Navigate href={returnTo} />` (href alone is a documented NavigateOptions form; the hack being removed is supplying both props and leaning on undocumented precedence) or a typed `<Navigate to="/dashboard" />` fallback. The adapter is the sole place a raw href reaches Navigate, and the existing e2e/join-return-to.spec.ts remains the real-router proof of the round trip; its long precedence rationale comment gets rewritten to describe the typed contract instead. The Navigate stub in packages/client/src/test/mock-react-router.tsx is updated to surface `search` and single-prop usage, and guard unit tests plus login-redirect tests follow. Explicitly out of scope: the render-behind stand-down branches in both guards (isGuestPath early returns) — they solve a distinct clobbering bug and must be preserved verbatim — and any change to the open-redirect validation rules themselves in login-redirect.ts.
directions.risks: Open-redirect regression if the safe-target validation is loosened or ends up applied on only one side of the round trip while refactoring where it lives; the returnTo value must still be rejected both entering /login and at resume. TanStack Router's search serializer may encode `returnTo` (a value containing `/`, `?`, `#`) differently from the current URLSearchParams-built href, so the exact-match assertion in e2e/page-objects/join.po.ts expectLoginWithReturnTo and any deep-linked login URLs need to tolerate or track the router's encoding. Accidentally simplifying away the guards' stand-down branches would reintroduce the destination-clobbering bug their comments document, and the only loud failure is the single E2E spec.
directions.leafNotes: Carry the verify-defect correction into the leaf's framing: `href` is a documented public NavigateOptions property usable instead of `to`; the undocumented part is only the precedence when both props are supplied simultaneously. The leaf must not claim href-only navigation is itself a hack — the adapter's fallback form deliberately uses it. Also carry: (a) GuestGuard wraps both /login and /register, so the validated-search read must work on both routes (add the same validateSearch to register-route.ts or read search non-strictly); (b) the E2E spec's header comment and the mock-react-router.tsx Navigate stub doc both describe the dual-prop convention and must be rewritten, not deleted — the E2E stays as the only real-router regression check; (c) buildLoginHref/readReturnTo may shrink to internals of the search contract, but isSafeReturnTo stays the single validation authority.

directions.direction: Add `transferCampaignOwnershipInputSchema` ({ campaignId, newOwnerUserId }) plus its inferred type to packages/shared/src/schemas/campaign-inputs.ts, then a `campaign.transferOwnership` mutation in packages/server/src/routers/campaign.ts that outputs `campaignDetailSchema` like `update`. Authorization must be owner-identity, not role: `assertCampaignDm` only checks member.role === "dm", so add an `assertCampaignOwner` helper in packages/server/src/utils/campaign-auth.ts that checks `campaign.ownerId === userId`, emits its own authz decision log event (e.g. authz.campaign.owner), and preserves the intentional NOT_FOUND-for-nonexistent / FORBIDDEN-for-non-owner mismatch semantics per docs/authorization.md. The mutation validates the target is an existing member of the campaign (and not the current owner), then atomically sets `ownerId` and promotes the target member's role to "dm" — a single Prisma nested write (`campaign.update` with `members.update` via the `campaignId_userId` unique) gives the transactionality without an interactive transaction; guard the owner check against a concurrent transfer race (e.g. condition the update on the current ownerId or re-check inside a transaction; read docs/CONCURRENCY.md first). After persistence, call `broadcastCampaignUpdate` and return `mapCampaignDetail`, matching the existing update mutation. Client side: add a TransferOwnershipSection in packages/client/src/components/campaign/settings/campaign-settings-panel.tsx next to DeleteCampaignSection, rendered only when `campaign.ownerId === user.id` (via useAuth — the settings tab is dm-gated in campaign-detail-page.tsx, which is not the same as owner) and other members exist; member picker from `campaign.members` excluding self, confirm dialog following the DeleteCampaignSection pattern, and on success `invalidateCampaignDetail` + `invalidateCampaignList`. Tests beside the code: a server router test (owner-only denial including a dm-role non-owner, non-member target rejection, atomic ownerId+role result, and that auth.deleteAccount succeeds after transfer) and a panel test extending campaign-settings-panel.test.tsx. Explicitly out of scope: demoting the old owner (they remain a dm member and can leave separately), transferring to non-members/invitees, any change to the deleteAccount blocking rule or its message, and moving campaign mutations into a service layer (router-inline matches the file's existing delete/update idiom). No Prisma schema change, so no migration.
directions.risks: The biggest correctness risk is gating on dm role instead of ownerId — a co-DM could then steal ownership, and after transfer the old owner's account deletion would cascade-delete nothing while a non-owner controls the campaign; a related race is two concurrent transfers or a transfer racing deleteAccount, so the ownerId write must be conditioned on the expected current owner. Secondary regressions: rewording the server error breaks the client's substring match on "Transfer or delete campaigns" in settings-page.tsx DangerZoneSection, and forgetting to promote the new owner's member role to dm leaves a campaign whose owner fails every assertCampaignDm check, bricking settings/delete for them.
directions.leafNotes: No verification defects to correct. Carry these grounding facts: (1) Campaign.owner relation is `onDelete: Cascade` (packages/server/prisma/schema.prisma ~line 1133), so ownership transfer is what actually preserves the campaign — worth asserting in the deleteAccount-after-transfer test. (2) The owner is seeded as a role-"dm" member in campaign.create, but nothing prevents multiple dm-role members, hence the owner-identity helper rather than assertCampaignDm. (3) The client settings tab renders CampaignSettingsPanel only for isDm viewers; the new section needs the additional ownerId === user.id check inside the panel. (4) Follow TDD and the repo's tRPC guide (docs/guides/) before writing the router; use existing test helpers from neighboring campaign router tests. (5) Keep the server message "Transfer or delete campaigns you own before deleting your account" unchanged, or update the settings-page.tsx substring match in the same commit.

Widening ProposeSummary.sourceKind is a type ripple into propose.test.ts/cli tests and any summary formatting assertions, and a type-aware-ts preview over broad globs may be slow enough to look like a hang.

directions.risks: Flipping listCombatLogs to newest-first inverts cursor semantics (gt→lt) and page composition, which will silently break any test or e2e assertion assuming oldest-first pages — the pagination tests must be rewritten alongside, not patched to pass. Removing `logs` from EncounterDetail changes the response shape of four combat envelopes plus encounter.get; test fixtures (fixtures-encounter.ts, fixtures-builders.test.ts) and ~80 server-test references to `logs` must be swept or the change stalls in the gate. Socket-driven invalidateEncounterCombatLogs refetches every loaded page of an infinite query on each new log, so long sessions with many loaded pages could refetch heavily during active combat — consider keeping only the first page fresh (or resetting pages on invalidation) rather than unbounded page refetch.

If any harness surface (knip entries, smoke subjects, lint-coverage-map) keys on the root file's export shape, deletion could trip a generated-surface check — evidence says none do (coverage map explicitly excludes root drift-ai entrypoints, smoke-subjects headers reference scripts/drift-ai/ paths only, knip treats scripts/*.ts as entries), but run harness:check after the change.
